Agentic engineering03

How the model reads

Two kinds of knowledge. The model brings what it was trained on — everything about your work has to arrive as text, every single request.

TRAINED IN · FROZEN
the weights
Language semantics, algorithms, idioms Library and framework APIs as of the training cutoff Patterns from public code — general, not particular to your repo
Does not change while you work — the model learns nothing from your session.
SENT AT RUN TIME · PER REQUEST
the context
Your instructions and your question The files, diffs and tool output the CLI collected Your conventions, your architecture, your names
This is the only part you control — and the whole subject of this talk.
context so far
→
predict
→
next token
→
appended, read again

One token at a time, and stateless — the client re-sends the whole conversation every turn. What feels like memory is re-reading.

Lost in the Middle

✕ forgotten
fact
BEGINNING MIDDLE END
arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172
Figure 1 · accuracy declines when the answer sits in the middle of the retrieved context, and recovers only near the start or end.

The beginning and the end of the window are read reliably. The middle is where a requirement quietly stops being applied.

The same fact in the middle is retained less well

Place critical instructions at the beginning or at the very end. The vertical axis is answer accuracy; the horizontal axis is the fact's position in the window.

Agentic engineering06

Quality vs. fill

UNDER 40%
Sharp
Follows rules, asks when unsure, edits narrowly — the same discipline you want in a test run
40 – 70%
Drifting
Forgets a convention, re-checks a case it already covered, starts padding coverage
OVER 70%
Sloppy
Contradicts earlier findings, invents test data, loops on the same failing case

The failure is gradual and quiet. By the time the session hits its limit, the test cases and reviews have been getting worse for a while.

/context
Read the meter.
What is filling the window right now, and how much is left
/compact
Replace the session with a summary.
Keeps the thread of the work, loses detail silently
/clear
Window back to zero.
New ticket, no residue; files and CLAUDE.md survive

Claude Code · Feature reference08

CLAUDE.md — always-on standards

Loaded in full at the start of every session, so every line is a recurring cost. Keep the facts that always apply; move the conditional ones somewhere that loads on demand.

LEAVE · EVERY SESSION
Role and boundaries: what this repo is, what not to touch The four commands: build, test, lint, run Naming and conventions the team actually enforces Where the truth lives: spec.md, adr/, docs/
EXTRACT · LOADED ON DEMAND
skills/ — multi-step procedures, pulled in when needed .claude/rules/ — rules scoped to one part of the repo hooks — anything that must happen every time, enforced permissions.deny — hard blocks, not polite requests
NO PRECEDENCE, ONLY CONCATENATION
Every file from the filesystem root down is concatenated, closest file read last — contradictions resolve arbitrarily
WRITE IT THE SECOND TIME
The same mistake twice, the same correction retyped, or something a new teammate would need
UNDER 200 LINES
Longer files cost more and are followed less; /init starts one, /doctor proposes trims
Claude Code · Feature reference09

Skills — on-demand expertise

A directory with a SKILL.md: name and description in the frontmatter, the procedure in the body. Only the name and description sit in the window all session — the body loads when the task matches.

.claude/skills/release/SKILL.md
---
name: release
description: cut a release —
  version bump, changelog, tag.
  Use when asked to ship or
  publish a version.
---
## Steps
1. Read CHANGELOG.md …
Level 1 · always loaded
Name and one-line description of every installed skill. Tens of tokens each, present all session.
Level 2 · on trigger
The body of SKILL.md enters the window when the description matches what you asked for.
Level 3 · if the skill asks
Linked reference files and templates, read only when needed. A script it runs costs nothing but its output.
THIRD PERSON, CONCRETE
Name the terms someone would actually use — that wording is what the match runs against
BUDGETS ARE REAL
Name and description under 1024 characters together; keep the body under roughly 500 lines
PERSONAL WINS
~/.claude/skills shadows .claude/skills on a name clash — the opposite of subagents

Claude Code · Feature reference11

Subagents — isolated delegated work

Each subagent runs in its own context window with its own system prompt, tool access and permissions. It does the noisy work in that window, and returns only the summary.

YOUR WINDOW
the returned summary
SUBAGENT WINDOW · DISCARDED
30 files, 4 searches, 2 failed test runs

It starts fresh: its own system prompt, the delegation message Claude writes, and your CLAUDE.md files. Not your conversation history, not the files already read, not the main conversation's auto memory.

THREE COME BUILT IN
Explore read-only search, Plan research in plan mode, general-purpose for multi-step work
ITS OWN EVERYTHING
Own model, own tool list, own permissions — a reviewer can be denied Write and Edit outright
RUNS BESIDE YOU
It works in the background while you keep going; the result arrives as a message when it finishes
Claude Code · Feature reference12

Hooks — event-driven automation

Shell commands fired on lifecycle events. They run whether or not the model felt like it.

SessionStart
Inject the branch, the ticket, today's state
PreToolUse
Inspect, and refuse, before the tool runs
PostToolUse
Format and lint every file the agent writes
Stop
Run the tests before the turn is called done
A rule in a file is a request. A hook is a guarantee, and it costs no context.
MATCHED TO A TOOL
Configured in settings.json against a matcher, so a formatter fires on Edit and Write only
EXIT 2 BLOCKS
JSON on stdin, exit code back: 0 passes, 2 blocks and feeds stderr to Claude to correct
YOUR CREDENTIALS
Hooks run as you, 60-second default timeout — review what you add; /hooks lists them
Claude Code · Feature reference13

MCP servers — external tools & integrations

A standard protocol for handing the agent tools it did not ship with. The repo gets a .mcp.json; the agent gets new verbs.

issue tracker
Read the ticket instead of you pasting it
database
Inspect a real schema, not a guess
browser
Drive the app it just changed
internal service
Your own API, exposed once for everyone

Every tool definition sits in the window from the first token, used or not — default to a CLI (gh, docker, psql, kubectl) where a good one already exists.

LOCAL · THE DEFAULT
Private to you, in this project only — where an experiment belongs
PROJECT · COMMITTED
.mcp.json at the repo root gives the team the same servers; Claude asks before running one
USER · EVERYWHERE
Available in all your projects; stdio, SSE or HTTP, OAuth through /mcp

What it costs, and when to pay

Each server publishes every tool it has, with schemas and descriptions. All of it loads up front, on every request, used or not.

WINDOW AT SESSION START
2
6
12
SERVERS CONNECTED
CLI THROUGH BASH
Costs nothing in the window until it is actually run Output is text, and you can filter it before it lands The agent has to know the command and its flags
Default where a good CLI exists for QA: playwright, newman, k6, axe, lighthouse.
MCP SERVER
Tool definitions sit in the window from the first token Results come back structured, and auth is handled once Discoverable — the agent is told what it can call
Worth the residency when there is no CLI, or when auth or structured results matter.

Skill 2 — Requirements Review

Looks at the context like a QA at grooming. Every requirement is run through the same four questions before it counts as covered.

FOUR QUESTIONS, EVERY REQUIREMENT
1. Can I test this?
2. What do I need for it?
3. Where can it break?
4. What isn't specified?

Gaps and contradictions go back to a person before anything is final.

context file
SKILL 2 · Requirements Review
numbered requirements · locked

Numbering is law: every later skill keys off these numbers — it never gets reshuffled downstream.

OPUS · HIGH + EXTENDED THINKING
Finding contradictions and gaps takes reasoning, not reading
HUMAN-IN-THE-LOOP
Gaps and contradictions are resolved with a person before the list locks
NUMBERING IS LAW
Every downstream skill reuses this exact numbering

Skill 6 — Implementation Code Review

The most complex skill in the pipeline. Takes the test cases and the PR summary, and checks every test case against the PR's code.

FOUR VERDICTS, PER TEST CASE
PASS
FAIL
QA — needs a human look
N/A — not implemented

Every FAIL and N/A ships with a reason, not just a label.

test cases + PR map

Skill 7 — Impact Analysis (Regression Review)

A regression pass over everything the PR touches, and everything near it. Did anything that used to work quietly break?

WHAT IT DOES
Developers write a short change-log file describing what they changed Cross-references that file against the PR diff, dependency by dependency Checks whether code that depends on the change still works with it
dev change-log + PR diff

Software QA · Skill chain23

The last link — manual verification

Not a skill — the tester. They inherit the checklist, the code-review verdicts and the regression report, and close the loop.

WHAT'S LEFT BY HAND
Verify the agent's own work, spot-check the PASS calls Walk every QA and N/A item the code review couldn't confirm Run the "interesting" extra checks the agent flagged along the way A few passes over the ticket's critical flows, for confidence
INHERITED FROM THE CHAIN
The checklist — Skill 3 The code-review verdicts and explanations — Skill 6 The regression report — Skill 7
Take a file in, do one job, hand a file out. Human-in-the-loop, not agentic hand-off — every result is visible before the next step runs.
INHERITS THREE FILES
The checklist, the code-review results, the regression report
CLOSES WHAT CODE REVIEW COULDN'T
Every QA and N/A item gets a human pass
NOT AGENTIC HAND-OFF
Human-in-the-loop by design; every step's result is visible before the next runs
Software QA · Lessons learned24

Failure modes — what went wrong

Four ways the pipeline broke in practice. Banning the behavior in the prompt never worked — only these fixes did.

FANTASIES
AI invents data when nothing anchors it — a checklist covers 10 requirements, 2 of them from nowhere.
Fix: tie every item to a quoted line from the requirement; flag what's unclear instead of covering it.
SEMANTIC DRIFT
Rewording quietly loses precision — "change the limit from 5 to 10" becomes "increase the limit," and the boundary values are gone.
Fix: preserve the original wording; no rephrasing without a human sign-off.
OVERLOAD
Five tasks in one prompt, and none of them done well — the same rule as one test case, one assertion.
Fix: split the overloaded skill into two narrower ones.
GARBAGE IN
A vague Jira ticket produces a vague chain: no PR linked, no code review; no impact notes, no regression pass.
Fix: push for ticket quality upstream — the pipeline can't out-think a bad input.

Make the failure visible — don't forbid it

Software QA · Agentic testing27

Planner — explore, then plan

Given an app and a scenario, the Planner explores the running app like a tester would, then writes a Markdown test plan — no code yet.

WHAT IT DOES
Navigates the app driven by the scenario, noting the real selectors and flows it finds along the way Explores edge states too — empty states, validation errors, unexpected redirects Writes a Markdown test plan: steps, expected results, and the locators it actually found
app + scenario
PLANNER
Markdown test plan

Planning from a live app beats planning from a spec — the plan only contains steps that actually exist in the UI.

EXPLORES BEFORE IT WRITES
Walks the real app, not just the ticket description
OUTPUT IS READABLE
A Markdown plan a human can review before any code is generated
NO CODE YET
Locks the scenario down before the Generator commits to selectors
Software QA · Agentic testing28

Generator — turn plans into tests

Takes the Planner's Markdown plan and turns every step into a real Playwright test, verifying each locator and assertion as it writes them.

WHAT IT DOES
Reads the test plan step by step, one scenario at a time Writes Playwright test code — actions, assertions, waits — matching each step Verifies every locator resolves and every assertion is checkable before moving on
Markdown test plan
GENERATOR
Playwright test file

Checks its own locators against the live app, so broken selectors get caught here, not in CI.

VERIFIES AS IT GOES
No locator ships unchecked
ONE PLAN IN, ONE FILE OUT
Same narrow-scope discipline as the QA skill chain
READY TO RUN
Output is a runnable Playwright test, not a draft
Software QA · Agentic testing29

Healer — run, then repair

Runs the generated tests, and when one fails, replays just the failing steps to work out whether the test is wrong or the app is — then repairs and reruns.

WHAT IT DOES
Runs the full Playwright test file and isolates any failing steps Replays only the failing steps — not the whole test — to save time Repairs the test (locator, timing, assertion) or flags a real app regression
Playwright tests
HEALER
passing test — or a flagged regression

Separates "the test is stale" from "the app broke" — only one of those is the Healer's job to fix.

REPLAYS, NOT RE-RUNS
Only the failing steps, to save time and tokens
FIXES THE TEST, FLAGS THE APP
A broken selector gets repaired; a real regression gets reported, not hidden
CLOSES THE LOOP
Plan → generate → run → heal, until the test is green or the bug is real
Recap30

What to take away

01How the model reads
The window is the whole state of the work — capacity has grown, but attention still runs out around 150–200 instructions Position matters: the middle of a long session is where things quietly get dropped Quality drifts long before the window is full — read /context before you trust the answer
02The Claude Code toolkit
CLAUDE.md for what's always true; skills, rules and hooks for what's only sometimes Subagents keep noise out of your window; a CLI costs nothing until it runs, an MCP server costs from the first token Five levers, one job each — use them together
03The QA skill chain
One Jira ticket, seven narrow skills, one file passed hand to hand — never the whole chat as context Isolation buys cheaper reruns, atomic checks, and a controllable failure surface The last step is still a human — closing what code review couldn't confirm
04Agentic testing
Plan from the live app, generate verified Playwright code, then heal — replaying only what actually failed Same discipline as the QA pipeline: one narrow job per stage, a file handed forward

Keep the index resident — keep the detail retrievable
